# Numerical Optimization — exam-eve notes

*typed at 1am, 9am exam. only wrote what i half-remember, sorry future me. abbrevs: gd = gradient descent, f' = derivative, grad = gradient vector, H = Hessian.*

## 1. Gradient descent (gd, steepest descent)

Use the negative gradient as the downhill direction. The learning rate controls the step size. A step that is too large can overshoot the minimum. update rule: x_{k+1} = x_k − alpha · grad f(x_k), alpha = step size / learning rate. prof writes eta for alpha. too small → crawls; too big → oscillate then diverge (saw it blow up in tutorial 3). stop when ||grad|| ~ 0. for convex f, gd converges to the global min (lecture 4 proof, not in these notes). every lecture sheet calls it gd but steepest descent is the formal name.

### gd tiny numerical example (tutorial 3, this part is solid)

f(x) = x^2, grad = 2x, x0 = 4, alpha = 0.1 → x1 = 4 − 0.1·8 = 3.2, x2 = 2.56, x3 = 2.048. each step multiplies the error by 0.8 (= 1 − 2·alpha): linear convergence, marches down to the min at 0. with alpha = 0.3 the factor is 0.4, same gd rule, shrinks faster. don't push alpha past 1 for this f or the factor flips past −1 and gradient descent diverges past the minimum instead of shrinking toward it. prof loves asking what the learning rate controls — step length vs speed in steepest descent.

## 2. Newton (Newton–Raphson)

Use the gradient and local curvature to choose an update. In one dimension the Newton update divides the derivative by the second derivative when that curvature is usable. for roots f(x) = 0: linearize at x_k, jump to where the tangent crosses zero: x_{k+1} = x_k − f(x_k)/f'(x_k). converges QUADRATICALLY near a simple root — correct digits roughly double each step, massively faster than gd, but only LOCAL: bad x0 → jumps to another root or blows up. breaks when f'(x_k) = 0 (it divides by it). sqrt trick: f(x) = x^2 − a.

### newton for MINIMIZATION — attempted derivation (INCOMPLETE!!)

want grad f(x) = 0, so run Newton–Raphson on g(x) = grad f(x). Jacobian of g is H (the matrix of second derivatives, entries d^2f/dx_i dx_j), so the step becomes x_{k+1} = x_k − H(x_k)^{−1} · grad f(x_k). scalar sanity check: f = x^2, H = 2, grad = 2x → x − 2x/2 = 0, lands on the min in one step, neat. BUT inverting a full n×n H every single step is total pain for big n. so the trick must be to keep some M_k ≈ H^{−1} cheaply and just re-fit it each step using the new s_k ... where do i even start — THAT'S WHERE I GOT STUCK. ask Arav before the exam, definitely 10 marks.

## 3. Line search (Armijo condition) — copied off slide 14, one line only

Armijo = sufficient decrease. Need to revise the condition. something about picking t_k so f(x_k + t·d_k) ≤ f(x_k) + c·t·grad f(x_k)^T d_k with c = 1e-4, then backtracking t → t/2 until it holds? unsure — no worked example written, that is exactly what i need to revise.

## 4. Quasi-Newton / BFGS (formula paste — zero intuition, missed the lecture)

BFGS updates a Hessian approximation using changes in position and gradient. pasted off the slide (inverse-Hessian version): H_{k+1} = (I − rho_k · s_k y_k^T) H_k (I − rho_k · y_k s_k^T) + rho_k · s_k s_k^T, rho_k = 1/(y_k^T s_k), s = position change, y = gradient change. start with H_0 = I presumably. DFP is "similar, terms swapped" — did not check. y^T s > 0 supposedly keeps it positive definite?? none of this is explained in my notes, just the formula.

*that's all i have. unit 2 matrices chapter i literally did not open — will lose marks, whatever.*

syllabus.raw:
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Gradient descent
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Newton’s method
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Armijo line search
Unit 1 (Unconstrained Optimization): Quasi-Newton / BFGS
Unit 2 (Linear Algebra): Gram–Schmidt
Unit 2 (Linear Algebra): Conjugate gradient

lesson.oneLiner: Move along the negative gradient: it points downhill only locally, and the learning rate decides how far one step goes - too large a step overshoots the minimum.
lesson.why: Your notes get the direction right but leave step size feeling arbitrary; the two What-would-you-do scenarios on this lesson show what actually changes when a large step lands on the far side of the valley.
lesson.analogy: Walking straight down a hillside in fog: each step follows the steepest local slope, and your stride length decides whether you reach the valley floor or fly past it.

steps.text: Use the negative gradient as the downhill direction, and the learning rate controls the step size.
A step that is too large can overshoot the minimum - shorten the candidate step before blaming the direction.
On f(x) = x^2 with alpha = 0.1 each gd step multiplies the error by 0.8 and marches down to the min.
Pick the direction first (steepest descent), then choose the step size - a fixed rate, or a line search that shrinks candidates until they decrease enough.
Stop when the gradient norm is small; if iterates bounce or climb, revisit the step size before anything else.

pitfalls.text: The direction only describes the slope close to where you are; a large step can still land uphill on the other side of the valley.
Push alpha too far and gd diverges past the minimum instead of shrinking toward it.

notesGaps: No step-size selection rule is connected to gd - the one Armijo line elsewhere is a bare note to revise.
The convex-convergence claim is stated without its conditions or proof.
lesson.takeaway: The direction tells you where to go. Step size controls how far you go. Armijo checks for sufficient decrease.

examQuestion.q: Why can a gradient descent step taken in a downhill direction still increase the objective, and what would you change first?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: The negative gradient is a local linear model of the slope; a large step leaves the region where that model holds and can land higher on the far side. Shrink the candidate step (or add a line search) before changing the direction.

lesson.oneLiner: A local curvature model helps choose the update.
lesson.why: Your notes derive the root version and start the minimization version; this card finishes the thought and marks the one distinction examiners probe: Newton uses curvature directly, BFGS updates an approximation.
lesson.analogy: Gradient descent feels the slope and shuffles; Newton reads the whole local bowl under its feet and steps toward its bottom.

steps.text: Use the gradient and local curvature to choose an update.
In one dimension the Newton update divides the derivative by the second derivative when that curvature is usable.
For minimization apply Newton to grad f(x) = 0; the Jacobian of grad f is the Hessian H.
Near the solution the quadratic model converges much faster than a first-order step; far from it, the model stops describing reality.

pitfalls.text: Newton is only local: a bad x0 can jump to another root or blow up - your own notes warn about this.
In n dimensions Newton re-inverts the full H every step; unusable curvature (a singular H) breaks the update.

notesGaps: The minimization derivation stops mid-thought - the cheap curvature update (the quasi-Newton idea) is never finished.
No worked numerical example of Newton appears anywhere in the notes.
lesson.takeaway: Newton uses curvature directly. BFGS updates an approximation.

examQuestion.q: State the Newton update for minimization and explain when it should not be used.
examQuestion.modelAnswer: x_{k+1} = x_k - H(x_k)^{-1} grad f(x_k), from applying Newton-Raphson to grad f = 0 with the Hessian as the Jacobian. Avoid it when curvature is unusable (H singular or indefinite) or the start is far from the solution, since convergence is only local.

lesson.oneLiner: Accept a candidate step when it produces sufficient decrease relative to the local slope and step size.
lesson.why: The notes keep exactly one line about Armijo and flag the condition for revision - which is the same test Scenario B on the gradient-descent lesson asks you to reason through.
lesson.analogy: A refund policy: not just 'did the price drop', but 'did it drop by at least the promised fraction for the distance you travelled'.

steps.text: Armijo = sufficient decrease.
The candidate step must beat the drop predicted by the local slope over that step - a smaller objective value alone is not the test.
Backtracking: start at t = 1 and shrink t (e.g. halve) until the condition holds.

pitfalls.text: Confusing 'f got smaller' with 'Armijo satisfied' - a tiny decrease can still fail the check.
Forgetting the slope term c * t * grad f(x_k)^T d_k turns the test into plain descent with no guarantee.

notesGaps: The notes say 'Need to revise the condition' and never state the full inequality with its constants.
No worked backtracking example exists in the notes.
lesson.takeaway: A lower objective value alone can still fail the test.

examQuestion.q: State the Armijo sufficient-decrease condition and explain why it exists.
examQuestion.modelAnswer: f(x_k + t d_k) <= f(x_k) + c * t * grad f(x_k)^T d_k with c in (0,1). It exists to reject candidate steps whose drop is too small relative to the predicted linear decrease, keeping line search from accepting near-flat moves.

lesson.oneLiner: Use changes in position and gradient to update a curvature approximation.
lesson.why: Your notes paste the BFGS formula with zero intuition and the Newton derivation breaks off exactly where this update should continue it - this card is the sentence your notes never finished.
lesson.analogy: Learning a door's weight by feel: each push and response teaches the model another bit, so you never need the spec sheet (the real Hessian).

steps.text: BFGS updates a Hessian approximation using changes in position and gradient.
The notes paste s_k and y_k as the position change and the gradient change inside the update formula.
Keep H_k as an inverse-curvature stand-in and re-fit it each step instead of inverting the true H every step.
Require y_k^T s_k > 0 (a decent line search helps) so the search direction stays downhill.

pitfalls.text: Reading the formula as magic: each term encodes one secant observation - the update reuses information from earlier steps.
Quoting DFP and BFGS interchangeably - your 'terms swapped' note is the other rank-two update; check before citing.

notesGaps: Only the pasted formula is recorded; nothing says what H_k approximates or why y^T s > 0 matters.
No convergence statement and no worked example.
lesson.takeaway: The update reuses information from earlier steps.

examQuestion.q: In one paragraph: what does the BFGS update replace in Newton's method, and what information does it use?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: BFGS replaces the per-step inversion of the true Hessian with an update to an inverse-Hessian approximation H_k, built from the observed change in position s_k = x_{k+1} - x_k and change in gradient y_k = g_{k+1} - g_k, keeping the secant relation H_{k+1} y_k = s_k.

lesson.oneLiner: Build orthogonal directions by subtracting projections onto directions you already built.
lesson.why: No matching passage in these notes - Unit 2 was never opened, so every line here is a Vertex explanation and the fastest place to bank easy marks.
lesson.analogy: Tasting-menu pairing: each new dish keeps only the flavour no earlier dish already brought, so nothing is a repeat.

steps.text: Keep the first vector, normalize it: q_1 = v_1 / ||v_1||.
For each later vector subtract its projections onto every q kept so far: u_k = v_k - sum_j (v_k . q_j) q_j.
Normalize u_k to q_k, then stack the q's as Q (coefficients as R) for the QR factorization.

pitfalls.text: Orthogonal does not mean unit length - orthonormal means both (zero dot product and length 1).
A vector already in the span gives u_k = 0; normalizing would divide by zero - the input was dependent.

notesGaps: No matching passage in these notes (Unit 2 matrices chapter was never opened).
lesson.takeaway: Orthogonal vectors have zero dot product. Orthonormal vectors also have unit length.

examQuestion.q: Apply the Gram-Schmidt process to v1 = (1, 1) and v2 = (2, 1) and give the orthonormal pair.

lesson.oneLiner: For a symmetric positive-definite linear system, build search directions conjugate with respect to the system matrix.
lesson.why: No matching passage in these notes, so everything here is a Vertex explanation. It reuses the gradient-descent idea but repairs the zig-zag by forbidding repeated downhill directions.
lesson.analogy: Walking a valley with a rule that each new direction never undoes the progress made along the earlier ones.

steps.text: Solve Ax = b by minimizing f(x) = 0.5 x^T A x - b^T x; A must be symmetric positive-definite.
Start along the negative gradient, then each new direction is conjugate to the previous ones with respect to A.
Step exactly along the current direction; on an n-dimensional problem the solution is reached in at most n steps (in exact arithmetic).

pitfalls.text: Conjugacy uses the matrix-weighted inner product d_i^T A d_j = 0, not the plain dot product.
In floating point it is a preconditioned iteration, not a literal n-step direct solver.

notesGaps: No matching passage in these notes (Unit 2 matrices chapter was never opened).
lesson.takeaway: Conjugacy uses the matrix-weighted inner product.

examQuestion.q: When does conjugate gradient apply, and how does its direction rule differ from gradient descent?
examQuestion.modelAnswer: CG applies to Ax = b with A symmetric positive-definite (or quadratics with such a matrix). Gradient descent repeats steepest-descent directions and zig-zags; CG makes each new direction A-conjugate to the old ones (d_i^T A d_j = 0), so each line search preserves earlier progress.
